records.our_prose: A documented traditional companion for strawberries (West Virginia University lists borage among strawberry companions; UC ANR notes growers tuck a few plants into beds to enhance flavor and yield). The reliable benefit is bee pollination of the berries; keep the large borage plants to the edges so they do not shade the low strawberries.

records.our_prose: Borage is not one of USU Extension's Table 1 vegetable rows, so this spring window follows the Group A (Hardy) February 15 date given to other cold-hardy, direct-sown crops for St. George. Sow shallow where the plant will grow, since it resents transplanting; blue star flowers and cucumber-flavored leaves follow in about 55 days, and the stand is cut through May. St. George's summers routinely reach 100°F in June, July, and August, per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation data, well past what this cool-preference annual tolerates, so growth stalls through the hottest stretch. A second direct sowing in early August, once the worst heat has broken, follows USU's general fall-gardening guidance for restarting cool-season crops (Fall Gardening in the St. George Area); this fall stand flowers from late September and is picked up to just ahead of the average November 1 first frost. It self-sows freely between rounds.

records.our_prose: Borage is grown for bloom, a top pollinator draw, and edible leaves and flowers, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as they would for produce. Harvest young, tender leaves before they turn too bristly, and pick fully open flowers on a dry day; pull off and discard the fuzzy green sepals behind each flower before eating. The leaves taste of cucumber and are used in salads, teas, and cool drinks; the blue flowers are a garnish and can be frozen into ice cubes. Use only unsprayed plants, and eat borage in moderation: the leaves contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which NC State notes can damage the liver and lungs, so use them only sparingly, and borage also has a diuretic effect in large amounts. Wear gloves when harvesting, since the stems and older leaves are prickly.

records.our_prose: Keep the soil evenly moist through germination and until seedlings are established, then water only when the soil dries; borage is notably drought-tolerant once established and resents constantly wet soil, which rots its roots. Water at the base and keep the foliage dry to limit powdery mildew.
